newsitem.title: USA: Valero seeks merger partner for gas unit.
newsitem.headline: Valero seeks merger partner for gas unit.

text.p: Valero Energy Corp. said Thursday it was looking for a merger partner for its natural gas unit in a transaction that could be valued at more than $1.4 billion.
The company said it had retained Lehman Brothers Inc. to help in soliciting interest from a list of 37 firms it had pinpointed as possible partners.

"By February we hope that we've selected someone. If they don't require an IRS tax ruling, we'd have a shareholders meeting in May and it could be done in May," Valero Chairman Bill Greehey told Reuters in an interview.
Greehey said Valero's move was part of an industry trend toward consolidation in which only the biggest players were expected to survive.
"If we ran business as usual, we'd get pretty well squeezed out," he said.
He said the expected transaction would be "stock for stock. They'd be acquiring all the Valero stock and in turn would give Valero shareholders some of their stock."

He said the gas unit, which includes a 7,500-mile pipeline system with a capacity of 3 billion cubic feet a day, was thought to be worth "$1.4 billion plus" based on the price paid in recent pipeline mergers.

Valero would spin off its refining and marketing operations into a separate company that would retain the Valero name, Greehey said. Its primary asset would be a 171,000 barrel-a-day refinery in Corpus Christi, Texas.

Greehey had been chairman of Valero, but was also given the title of chief executive on Thursday because of the resignation of president and CEO Joe Becraft. Becraft served in those positions only since July, but left because his expertise is in natural gas, not refining, Greehey said.
Valero was moving quickly because of concern that these kinds of transactions will be made taxable in 1998 and also for fear of getting left without a suitable partner, Greehey said.
"There are so many mergers, we felt like if you don't get out there pretty quick, the right merger partner is not going to be there because they've already found someone else," he said.
Of the 37 companies Valero believes most likely to be interested in a deal, 16 are electric utilities, Greehey said.

"I think you're going to see more and more of those mergers (between natural gas firm and utilities)," he said. "They're (utilities) looking for the culture of a non-regulated company and someone that can manage their fuel costs -- and the largest market for natural gas is electricity generation."
